overview: Some fungi live a double life, switching form entirely depending on temperature — and that switch is exactly what lets them invade human tissue.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: Fungi that exist as a mold at room temperature (25°C) in the environment and convert to a yeast (or spherule) form at body temperature (37°C) in tissue.
aspects.valueB: Fungi that maintain a single morphological form regardless of temperature — either always a mold or always a yeast.

aspects.label: Temperature-Dependent Morphology
aspects.valueA: Thermally dimorphic — mold form in the environment, yeast/spherule form in the host.

aspects.label: Examples
aspects.valueA: Histoplasma capsulatum, Blastomyces dermatitidis, Coccidioides (mold to spherule), Sporothrix schenckii.
aspects.valueB: Aspergillus species (always mold), Candida albicans (always yeast, aside from pseudohyphae).

aspects.label: Clinical Significance of the Switch
aspects.valueA: The switch to yeast/spherule form at body temperature is often required for virulence and tissue invasion.
aspects.valueB: No comparable temperature-triggered virulence switch; pathogenicity depends on other factors like immune status.

aspects.label: Geographic Distribution
aspects.valueA: Many are geographically restricted (endemic mycoses tied to specific soil/climate niches).
aspects.valueB: More globally ubiquitous distribution (e.g. Aspergillus is found worldwide).

aspects.label: Laboratory Safety Consideration
aspects.valueA: Mold-phase cultures of dimorphic fungi can be highly infectious via inhaled spores — require biosafety cabinet handling.
aspects.valueB: Safety precautions vary by species but generally lack this specific mold-phase inhalation hazard tied to the same dimorphic mechanism.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: Changes form with temperature, tied to virulence.
aspects.valueB: Maintains one form regardless of temperature.
